title: Exploring Turn-taking Cues in Multi-party Human-robot Discussions about Objects
study_type: Technical system description combined with a field-trial analysis of 373 museum interactions, including systematic manipulation of the robot's turn-taking cues and attention.
study_setting: Field deployment in the Swedish National Museum of Science and Technology over 9 days in November 2014, with visitors playing in groups of two.
sample_size: Data were recorded from 373 interactions with the system, averaging 4.5 minutes each; the total number of individual participants is not explicitly stated.
participant_characteristics: Museum visitors of mixed ages: adults playing with adults (40%), children playing with adults (27%), and children playing with children (33%) of interactions.
task: Two visitors and Furhat played a collaborative card-sorting game, discussing and sorting five cards by a criterion (e.g., invention order or running speed), with an average interaction length of 4.5 minutes.
group_size: Three per session: two visitors plus one Furhat robot head.
n_humans: 2 visitors per session.
measurement_tools: Kinect-based tracking of users' head pose, speech recognition word and concept error rates on 9 transcribed and annotated dialogs, manual annotation of speech segments on a four-grade scale, and chi-square tests on user speech after turn-taking cues.
significant_measures: Gazing away during a turn-taking cue significantly reduced the likelihood of user speech (main effect of gaze, p<0.001). Without cues, users continued speaking 33.8% of the time, versus 14.8% with the right combined cues. Furhat's attention target also strongly influenced which user responded (p<0.001).
framing: Robotic gaze-based attention
framing_definition: The paper does not explicitly define robotic gaze or attention. It operationalises attention as Furhat's target (idle, item, user, or all), maintained by an Attention Flow that moves its gaze and neck.
framing_role: Gaze and attention serve turn-taking: the robot signals it is claiming the floor with gaze-away plus a cue (filled pause, breath, or smile), and gaze selects the next speaker (addressee selection). The robot also acts as a passive side participant through backchannels.
effects: Furhat's attention target strongly influenced which user responded after its questions (p<0.001). When the targeted user was looking back at Furhat, that user was more likely to take the turn (p<0.05).
implementation: Built in IrisTK with two parallel controllers: a Dialog Flow for turn-taking and an Attention Flow that maps 3D target positions to neck and gaze movements. A Situation model fuses Kinect head tracking, close-talking microphones with two parallel cloud ASR recognizers, and touch-table events; a randomized belief model drives responses.
embodiment: Furhat robot head: an animated face back-projected on a translucent mask, with a mechanical neck.
embodiment_influence: The paper argues that 2D animated agents suffer from the Mona Lisa effect because agent and user do not share physical space. Citing prior work, it states Furhat's back-projection on a 3D mask improves turn-yielding accuracy.
tldr: The paper presents a multi-party card-sorting dialog system built on the Furhat robot head, which was exhibited in a museum and used by 373 interactions. Field data showed that gaze-away plus a filled pause, smile, or breath reduced users' likelihood of continuing to speak, and that Furhat's attention target strongly influenced which user responded.

title: Are you talking to me? Improving the Robustness of Dialogue Systems in a Multi Party HRI Scenario by Incorporating Gaze Direction and Lip Movement of Attendees
study_type: Experimental proof-of-concept user study with a humanoid robot in a multiparty interaction, in which addressee recognition approaches were evaluated against ground-truth annotation.
study_setting: Laboratory-style smart-home apartment (Cognitive Service Robotics Apartment, CSRA), with participants seated around a table, on a sofa, and in armchairs.
sample_size: 15 participants (2 female and 13 male) took part, across 5 trials totalling about 53 minutes of interaction.
participant_characteristics: Participants were German native speakers; 2 were female and 13 male. No age or prior robot experience is reported.
task: Participants picked a task slip from the table (e.g., turn lights on/off, ask the time, request information), told another participant to issue it to the robot, and that participant had to gain the robot's attention and repeat the request. A typical trial took about 10 minutes.
group_size: One robot (Meka) with six people per session, as described for the experimental setup (three at the table, one on the sofa, two in armchairs).
n_humans: 6 participants per session, per the described setup (three at the table, one on the sofa, two in armchairs).
measurement_tools: Addressee recognition classifications were compared with a ground-truth annotation of each dialogue act, using a 2x2 confusion matrix to compute accuracy, recall, precision, and the diagnostic odds ratio (DOR). Recordings were annotated in ELAN.
significant_measures: No statistical tests are reported. Mutual gaze kept recall at 93% and raised accuracy to 89%, against an 84% baseline, while lips-or-gaze reached 91% accuracy and the highest DOR (91.1 versus 5 for the baseline).
framing: Robotic gaze-based attention
framing_definition: The authors do not give a general definition of gaze or attention. Operationally, mutual gaze is assumed when a person's gaze direction stays within a range of α around the robot's head, and the attention management system is based on hierarchical prioritization of multi-modal sensor input streams.
framing_role: Mutual gaze at the end of an utterance serves as a turn-yielding cue that helps the robot decide whether an utterance was addressed to it. Attention management lets the robot observe and turn toward persons outside its field of view.
effects: Effects were measured only on addressee recognition performance, not on the people themselves. Attention management was reported to facilitate addressee recognition when not all participants are visible, and lip-movement verification decreased false positive addressee recognitions.
implementation: Autonomous system on the Meka robot: an attention manager arbitrates prioritized input streams (face detection, then sound source, then saliency) with override and gaze controllers over ROS/RSB. Addressee recognition uses a gaze detector with facial landmarks, classifying speaking from inner-lip distance variance and mutual gaze; speech recognition uses Sphinx and dialogue uses InproTK and Pamini.
embodiment: Meka, a humanoid M1 Mobile Manipulator with an omni-directional base, lift-controlled torso, two arms with four-fingered hands, and 37 motor-powered joints (including 2 in the head).
embodiment_influence: Head movements of the robot caused motion blur, so gaze and lip features were sometimes not detected at the relevant moment. The attention system was designed to be exchangeable across platforms, such as NAO or iCub.
tldr: The paper presents the humanoid robot Meka with an attention management system that prioritizes face, sound, and saliency cues so it can look at people, including those outside its view. In a multiparty study with 15 participants in 5 trials, mutual gaze at utterance end improved addressee recognition accuracy and precision, while lip movements alone performed poorly. Combining gaze OR lip movement gave the best accuracy and odds ratio.

It reports that attention management facilitates addressee recognition (RQ3b) and uses the humanoid Meka robot (RQ5a, RQ5b).

title: Social Robot Haru Assisting Dynamic Group Discussion with Autonomous Eye Gaze Behavior
study_type: Technical system development combined with an experimental user study comparing three conditions using physical Haru. The autonomous gaze policy was trained in a Gazebo simulation before being transferred to the robot.
study_setting: Simulated Gazebo environment for policy training, and a user study with physical Haru in which groups discussed a topic seated beside Haru on a table. The paper does not name a specific room or venue beyond recruiting from a university campus.
sample_size: 50 participants in total: 27 recruited for the user-perspective part (21 valid responses analysed) and 23 third-party evaluators.
participant_characteristics: University campus participants. User-perspective group: aged 21-28 (mean 23.70, SD 1.438), 51.86% male, 40.74% female, 7.40% undisclosed. Third-party group: aged 20-27 (mean 23.41, SD 1.343), 60.87% male, 34.78% female, 4.35% undisclosed.
task: Groups of three discussed a topic given by the instructor beside Haru, with one assumed extroverted, one introverted and one new user joining. Each group experienced three conditions: chatbot only, chatbot plus balancing and welcoming, and chatbot plus balancing, welcoming and autonomous gaze. Discussion duration is not stated.
group_size: Three people plus one robot per session: two conversing users and one new comer joining, with Haru.
n_humans: Three human participants per session in the user study (two conversing users plus one new comer). In simulation, Haru randomly observed 2-4 users per training episode.
measurement_tools: Godspeed questionnaire for anthropomorphism, animacy, likability and perceived intelligence, plus satisfaction and eight custom conversation-experience items, all rated on 7-point Likert scales. Also two open-ended questions, Cronbach's alpha reliability checks, and ANOVA with Fisher LSD post-hoc tests.
significant_measures: User ratings: Condition 3 scored significantly higher than Conditions 1 and 2 on all five measures (p<0.01), while Condition 2 beat Condition 1 only on satisfaction. Third-party ratings: Condition 3 beat both on all five measures, and Condition 2 beat Condition 1 on satisfaction, animacy and likability.
framing: Robotic gaze
framing_definition: The paper gives no formal definition of gaze or attention. It describes Haru's gaze behaviours as designed to replicate human gaze movements, including vestibulo-ocular movement, during face-to-face interaction.
framing_role: Gaze is used to show politeness and to direct gaze to the current speaker, a less-engaged user (to encourage participation) or a new joiner. Haru shifts gaze between speakers via eyeball movement when they are close, and via body rotation otherwise.
effects: Compared with chatbot-only Haru, adding balancing and welcoming behaviour improved satisfaction and some perceptions, and adding autonomous gaze further improved anthropomorphism, animacy, likability, perceived intelligence and satisfaction in both user and third-party ratings.
implementation: Gaze policy learned autonomously with soft actor-critic deep reinforcement learning in a Gazebo simulation, with a state of user positions, speaking indicators and motor angle, and actions of body rotation or eyeball movement, then transferred to physical Haru. Speech uses Google ASR, the Kimi LLM and TTS, and user positions and speaking are detected with Azure Kinect.
embodiment: Tabletop social robot Haru with five degrees of freedom: base rotation, neck tilt, eye movement, eye rotation and eye tilt. Each eye is a 3-inch TFT screen bordered by addressable LED strips, and an LED matrix simulates mouth movements.
embodiment_influence: Eye-screen geometry limits the eye centre to a range to avoid an impolite whites-of-eyes look, and eye positions reset during body turns. Because Haru is fixed on a desktop, the state uses only the azimuth direction, and motor rotation is limited to a safe range.
tldr: The authors built a system for the social robot Haru to assist dynamic group discussion, combining LLM-based chat, a balancing and welcoming module, and an autonomous eye-gaze module learned by deep reinforcement learning in simulation and transferred to the physical robot. In a study with 50 participants in groups of three, adding balancing and welcoming improved satisfaction and perceived politeness over a chatbot-only Haru, and adding autonomous gaze further improved anthropomorphism, animacy, likability, perceived intelligence and satisfaction.

title: Social Robot Haru Imitating Human Gaze for Attention and Turn-Taking Coordination in Multi-party Conversation
study_type: Technical system description combined with an experimental within-subjects user study in which all 22 participants experienced both conditions (dialogue only vs. dialogue plus autonomous gaze).
study_setting: Real-world user study with participant pairs recruited from a university campus; gaze policy was trained beforehand in a Gazebo simulation.
sample_size: 22 participants (11 groups of 2).
participant_characteristics: Aged 22 to 27 years, 15 males and 7 females, university campus recruits; 59.1% had experience in social robotics and 40.9% had no relevant experience.
task: Pairs of participants talked on a topic assigned by an instructor while interacting with Haru; each group experienced both the dialogue-only condition and the dialogue plus autonomous gaze condition in randomized order, with a short break between them.
group_size: 2 humans plus 1 robot (Haru) per session.
n_humans: 2 per session.
measurement_tools: Godspeed questionnaire (anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, perceived intelligence, perceived safety), selected PSI items, four custom satisfaction questions and two custom willingness-to-use questions, all on 5-point Likert scales, analysed with Cronbach's alpha and paired t-tests.
significant_measures: Haru was rated significantly better in Condition 2 than Condition 1 on all GODSPEED and PSI dimensions (paired t-tests, p<0.01; e.g., anthropomorphism t = -8.737). Participants also reported significantly higher enjoyment, perceived attentive listening, overall satisfaction, willingness to re-engage, and willingness to use and recommend Haru in Condition 2 (p<0.01).
framing: Robotic gaze-based attention
framing_role: Haru's gaze is used to follow the current speaker and to orient toward the middle between users when both are talking or silent, coordinating attention and turn-taking in the group conversation.
effects: Participants rated Haru more favourably with gaze behaviour: they preferred it when it maintained mutual gaze, and were more inclined to use it in daily life and to recommend it to others in Condition 2 (p<0.01).
implementation: Gaze policy learned with GAIL from human expert demonstrations, using relative azimuth angles and speaking status as state and head-rotation change as action; trained in a Gazebo simulation for 1500 episodes and transferred to the real robot. Users were tracked with an Azure Kinect for skeleton and sound localization, and dialogue used ASR, ChatGPT and TTS.
embodiment: Haru, a desktop social robot placed on a tabletop; its gaze direction is produced by rotation restricted to a predefined range of [−90°, 90°].
embodiment_influence: Hardware constraints restricted Haru's rotational movement to [−90°, 90°], which defined the range of its gaze actions in the study.
tldr: The paper presents the social robot Haru, which learns human-like gaze from real-world demonstrations using GAIL (trained in simulation and transferred to the robot) and uses ChatGPT for open-domain dialogue, so that gaze coordinates attention and turn-taking between two users. In a 22-participant study (11 pairs), adding the autonomous gaze module made Haru significantly better rated on social intelligence, satisfaction, and willingness to use than dialogue alone.

title: The Power of a Glance: Evaluating Embodiment and Turn-Tracking Strategies of an Active Robotic Overhearer
study_type: Experimental video-rating study in which participants judged videos of a NAO robot overhearing recorded conversations under six behaviour models.
study_setting: Participants watched the robot videos one at a time on a computer screen with headphones, using a GUI with a single play button; the paper does not name a lab or field setting.
sample_size: 29 participants.
participant_characteristics: Students or otherwise affiliated with Bielefeld University, all native German speakers; mostly female (six male), aged 17-55 (mean 24, median 23). Two had prior HRI study experience and three had other robot experience.
task: Participants watched 18 videos (six per audio part) of a NAO robot acting as an active overhearer of recorded dyadic conversations, then rated how well it followed the discussion and how close its behaviour was to a human's. Each video covers an interaction part of about 60-65 seconds.
group_size: Two humans in the recorded conversation plus one NAO robot as overhearer; the robot is not a live participant and the raters are not part of the interaction.
n_robots: One NAO robot per session, taking the role of an active overhearer.
n_humans: Two humans per interaction (a dyadic conversation); the stimuli were drawn from three dyadic interactions.
measurement_tools: Two custom questions rated on unbounded scales (how well the robot followed the discussion; how close its behaviour was to a human's), analysed with ranking and z-scores, Friedman and Wilcoxon tests; a post-experiment questionnaire included a 0-5 task difficulty rating.
significant_measures: Moving-eye models were rated significantly higher than their fixed-eye counterparts for all pairs (Friedman χ2=75.88, p<0.001; Wilcoxon post-hoc, Bonferroni-adjusted α=0.0033). Oracle models (PRD, RCT) clearly outperformed the random baseline (RND), most strongly with moving eyes, while PRD and RCT did not differ significantly.
framing: Robotic gaze
framing_definition: The paper gives no formal definition of gaze or attention; it describes gaze as the eyes rotating so the pupil turns toward a target, which is distinct from head turning.
framing_role: As an active overhearer, the robot turns its head and eyes toward the currently active speaker, following the turn-taking structure so that it signals to other observers that it is attentive and engaged.
effects: Moving eyes considerably increased ratings of the robot's attentiveness, ability to follow the discussion, and naturalness. The randomly timed model with moving eyes was rated higher than the fixed-eye reactive and predictive models, though these differences were not statistically significant.
implementation: Eyes are two Arduino-driven TFT screens showing pupils; pupil displacement is computed from a linear regression fitted to eye-tracker data, with separate head and eye controllers. Overhearer models (RND, RCT, PRD) use turn timing from transcripts, so they are oracle models rather than autonomous.
embodiment: Aldebaran NAO humanoid robot with a pair of small displays (1.77 inch) as eyes behind a paper mask with a 3D nose. The NAO head has only yaw and pitch degrees of freedom and cannot tilt.
embodiment_influence: The physical 3D mask and eyes placed in physical space let the robot avoid the Mona Lisa effect, and the NAO head's lack of tilt meant the pupil model ignored tilted head posture.
tldr: The authors equipped a NAO robot with moving-pupil eyes and tested, through a video-rating study with 29 participants, how an active overhearer of recorded dyadic conversations should time gaze and head turns. title: Skantze et al. - 2015 - A Collaborative Human-Robot Game as a Test-bed for Modelling Multi-party, Situated Interaction
study_type: Technical/system description: a demonstration paper presenting a test-bed for collecting data and testing models of multi-party situated human-robot interaction. The system was deployed in a museum and data was logged.
study_setting: Field deployment in a public museum: the Swedish National Museum of Science and Technology, where the system was exhibited for nine days in November 2014.
sample_size: The paper reports 373 recorded interactions with the system, averaging 4.5 minutes each. The total number of participants is not explicitly stated.
participant_characteristics: Museum visitors of mixed ages, including both children and adults. No further demographic details are reported.
task: Two visitors at a time play a collaborative card sorting game with Furhat, sorting cards (e.g., inventions by year or animals by speed) on a touch table while discussing the solution together. After completing one game, players could choose to continue; 58 of the pairs who completed the first game chose to do so.
group_size: Each interaction session includes two human visitors and one robot (Furhat), i.e., three participants in total.
n_robots: One robot (the Furhat robot head) per interaction session.
n_humans: Two humans (visitors) per interaction session.
measurement_tools: The paper does not describe questionnaires or outcome instruments. Data was recorded from the interactions, and users' attentional behaviour is approximated by head pose.
significant_measures: No statistical results are reported. Qualitative claims include that the system proved fairly robust against speech recognition errors, that children and adults enjoyed the game, and that 58 pairs chose to continue playing.
framing: The paper uses the concepts of visual focus of attention (VFOA) and joint attention, with Furhat's attention directed to targets such as users or cards. It does not use the term robotic gaze-based attention explicitly.
framing_role: Furhat's gaze is used to maintain joint attention on the cards and exclusive mutual gaze with users. Users' head pose determines whether they are addressing Furhat or each other, which decides whether Furhat contributes or only gives backchannels.
effects: No effects of Furhat's gaze were measured in this paper. The authors state, citing prior work, that shared visual focus of attention has a clear effect on turn-taking behaviour.
implementation: Autonomous system built in the IrisTK framework. A Kinect V2 tracks users' heads and hands, a Situation model maps events to a common 3D representation, and an Attention Flow statechart moves Furhat's neck and gaze toward targets. Speech is recognized by two parallel cloud-based recognizers using close-talking microphones.
embodiment: The Furhat robot head, which has an animated face back-projected on a translucent mask and a mechanical neck. It signals focus of attention through a combination of head pose and eye gaze.
embodiment_influence: The paper states that Furhat's 3D design makes exclusive mutual gaze and gaze-target inference possible. It does not compare different embodiments.
tldr: The paper presents a collaborative card-sorting game in which two visitors and the Furhat robot head jointly discuss cards on a touch table, with Furhat's gaze directed to maintain joint attention. It is proposed as a test-bed for collecting data and building data-driven models of gaze and turn-taking, but no gaze effects were measured.

title: The furhat back-projected humanoid head–lip reading, gaze and multi-party interaction
study_type: Experimental: three lab-based experiments (lip reading perception, gaze perception, and multi-party turn-taking), plus a technical description of the Furhat back-projected head and an uncontrolled public museum deployment.
study_setting: Controlled lab environments for the three experiments, and a public museum setting (London Science Museum Robotville exhibition) for the field observation.
sample_size: Study I used 10 normal hearing subjects, Study II used 18 subjects, and Study III used two sets of five subjects (ten subjects in total). The museum exhibition involved thousands of visitors.
participant_characteristics: Study I subjects were normal hearing with normal or corrected to normal vision; Study II subjects had normal or corrected to normal vision. Museum visitors included many children. The paper does not report further demographic details.
task: In the lab, participants identified acoustically degraded Swedish sentences with a lip-synced head, placed a tagging object on the grid square they believed Furhat was gazing at, and answered route questions from an agent in a multi-party dialog. In the museum, visitors answered Furhat's survey questions about the future of robots over four days.
group_size: Study III: five human subjects plus one animated agent per session. Public exhibition: Furhat interacted with two users at a time, with two podiums and microphones.
n_robots: One robot head (Furhat) or one animated agent per interaction session.
n_humans: Study III: five subjects per session. Public exhibition: two users present at a time in the two-user condition.
measurement_tools: Sentence intelligibility accuracy (words correctly identified) in Study I; perceived gaze location on a grid, with angles and distances computed from a geometric model in Study II; manually annotated video turn-taking data, confusion matrix and response times in Study III.
significant_measures: Study III: turn-taking accuracy targeting the intended subject was 53% in the 2D condition and 84% in the 3D condition. Response time was significantly shorter in 3D (1.38 s) than in 2D (1.85 s), F(1)=15.821, p<0.001. Study I found Furhat significantly more intelligible than the flat screen.
framing: The paper does not give a formal definition of robotic gaze-based attention. It frames the topic as robotic gaze and its perception, with Furhat directing its attention using eye gaze and head pose and the Mona Lisa effect as the central concept.
framing_definition: No explicit definition is given. The paper describes the Mona Lisa effect: because a 2D agent is not spatially co-present, either all observers perceive it as looking at them or none do.
framing_role: Gaze serves turn-taking control, addressee selection and deictic reference. Gaze is used to address a particular person and to regulate multiparty dialogue turn-taking.
effects: On 2D displays, the Mona Lisa effect limits gaze-based turn-taking. A 3D back-projected head improved turn-taking accuracy and reduced response time. In the museum, open questions were answered by the addressee in 92.2% of cases, and Furhat's lip-synced face was more intelligible than a flat screen.
implementation: In Study III gaze shifts were controlled by a Wizard-of-Oz setup. In the museum, Furhat's behavior was autonomous, using handheld microphones, ultrasound proximity sensors and audio-level comparison to choose the addressee, with the IrisTK toolkit.
embodiment: Furhat is a back-projected, human-like robot head: a micro projector projects an animated face onto a 3D-printed mask, mounted on a pan-tilt-roll neck. The animated eyes have separately controllable pupils, irises and eyelids.
embodiment_influence: The physical 3D mask, compared with a flat screen, eliminated the Mona Lisa effect and made gaze exclusive to one person. The static mask also enlarged the perceived lips, which may explain the higher intelligibility. Calibration of gaze may need to differ by robot design.
tldr: The paper presents Furhat, a back-projected humanoid head, and three experiments on lip reading, gaze perception and multi-party turn-taking, plus a museum deployment. title: On the Benefit of Independent Control of Head and Eye Movements of a Social Robot for Multiparty Human-Robot Interaction
study_type: The study combines an analysis of human pilot gaze and head behaviour in a recorded three-party conversation with an online crowdsourced subjective evaluation of four head-eye coordination policies on a Furhat robot.
study_setting: The evaluation was conducted online as a third-party video rating study. The interaction data come from the RoboTrio corpus of a collaborative word game recorded with an iCub robot.
sample_size: 50 participants' submissions were analysed in the online evaluation, after 51 people completed it and one submission was rejected.
participant_characteristics: Online evaluation participants were French speakers aged 18 to 60 residing in France, Belgium or Switzerland, with a balanced number of females and males. The recorded human players in the corpus were pairs of men.
task: Players played a collaborative word game (Unanimo) with a robot animator in the recorded corpus. In the evaluation, subjects rated 15 short clips (about 10.5 seconds on average) selected from five annotated sequences.
group_size: Each interaction session involved two human players and one robot teleoperated by a human animator. The evaluation clips show only the virtual robot with the participants' soundtracks in stereo.
n_robots: One robot per interaction session. In the corpus this was an iCub teleoperated by a pilot, and in the evaluation clips a virtual Furhat robot.
n_humans: Two human players per interaction session, plus the human animator who teleoperates the robot.
measurement_tools: Participants rated the perceived naturalness of each clip on a 0 to 100 slider scale in the HEMVIP interface and then completed a general questionnaire about their familiarity with robots. Gaze and head focal points were also annotated from the corpus using GMM classification and OpenFace.
significant_measures: Policy significantly affected naturalness ratings (chisq(3)=744.53, p<0.0001). The EyesHead policy was rated significantly higher than the others, while Furhat and EyesOnly did not differ from each other but were rated significantly lower than HeadOnly and EyesHead.
framing: The authors frame robotic gaze as a combination of head and eye movements, where the robot's gaze generation involves identifying where to focus attention and a control policy that directs attention through body segments, with the head treated as an attention vector.
framing_definition: The authors state that gaze is essentially a combination of eye and head movements with their own kinematics, and that gaze is the addition of head and eye movements whose kinematics differ.
framing_role: Gaze and head orientation regulate multiparty conversation, contributing to addressee identification and next speaker identification, and the head orientation helps communicate to whom the robot is addressing.
effects: Driving only the eyes or only the head was rated less natural than replaying the original human behaviour with both channels. The Default Furhat policy, which aligns eyes and head at the end of the movement, obtained low scores compared with the other policies.
implementation: Gaze targets and head movements were taken from a teleoperated iCub recording and replayed on a Furhat robot under four head-eye policies. The Furhat controller computes eye trajectories toward targets, and clips were rendered with the Furhat simulator and presented via HEMVIP.
embodiment: The data were collected with an iCub robot, which reproduces three degrees of freedom each for head and eyes plus articulated lips and jaw. The evaluation used a virtual Furhat robot head.
embodiment_influence: The authors note that some robots cannot move their eyes or neck freely, which limits gaze models to head-only or eye-only vectors. They also attribute the poor Furhat policy results partly to the Furhat head moving slowly with a large amplitude.
tldr: The authors analysed a three-party teleoperated conversation and found that the pilot's head contribution to gaze was weaker when addressing both players than when addressing one. An online evaluation with 50 participants on a Furhat robot showed that a policy replaying the human's decoupled head and eye movements was rated most natural.

It also describes how the policies were implemented on a Furhat robot using iCub-based data (RQ4), names the iCub and Furhat embodiments (RQ5), and discusses how Furhat head speed and amplitude affected results (RQ6).

title: Developing an Interactive Gaze Algorithm for Android Robots
study_type: Technical system description: the authors implemented an autonomous gaze algorithm on an android robot and informally observed people's reactions to it at an exhibition.
study_setting: The demonstration took place at the Robot-world 2015 international robot exhibition in South Korea, in a noisy exhibition center that prevented voice interaction.
sample_size: Around 500 people in total came to observe the robot.
task: The autonomous gaze algorithm was demonstrated to visiting observers at a robot exhibition, where the robot gazed at detected faces and occasionally gave an introduction, sang and danced to entertain groups.
group_size: The paper describes groups of observers including single observers with onlookers, large groups, and parents with children, but does not report exact people or robot counts per session.
n_robots: One robot was used: the EveR-4 android.
measurement_tools: Only system and technical metrics are reported, including the system frame rate and face detector processing time. Observer reactions were noted informally, and no questionnaire or formal coding is reported.
significant_measures: The system ran at about 3 frames per second, and the head and eyes converged on the target after 0.5 and 0.2 s respectively. In the single-observer example, a newly detected face received importance 0.96 while the earlier observer dropped to 0.04.
framing: The paper frames its gaze algorithm as a way to acknowledge multiple participants and use attention shifts to support proper turn-taking, as a precursor to multi-party conversation.
framing_definition: The paper does not give a formal definition of gaze-based attention. It states that an importance value is assigned to each detected face based on how long it was detected and its distance to the robot.
framing_role: Gaze divides attention among everyone present to acknowledge them and set up a platform for inviting conversation. It also helps ensure smooth transitions as people enter and leave the conversation.
effects: The authors report that the robot gazed at observers as expected and engaged them according to proximity and duration, but interaction was somewhat limited. They also report that randomly used facial expressions led to a greater sense of interaction overall.
implementation: The system is autonomous: an RGB-D camera with a face detector and tracker finds faces, 3D centroids are taken from the point cloud, and importance is a linear combination of distance and frames tracked. The highest-importance centroid becomes the gaze target, sent from a gaze PC to the robot onboard PC, which drives head and eye motion. An operator could switch the robot between interactive and non-interactive modes.
embodiment: The robot is the EveR-4 android, which wore a dress and was made up to resemble a real woman. Its body remained still while its head and eyes gazed at people and its face made random expressions such as winking, smiling and blinking.
tldr: The authors implemented an autonomous gaze algorithm on the EveR-4 android that gives each detected face an importance value based on its distance and how long it has been tracked, then gazes at the highest-importance person. title: Identifying the Focus of Attention in Human-Robot Conversational Groups
study_type: Technical system description with evaluation: an HMM-based focus-of-attention method tested on the public Babble dataset and in a live laboratory experiment with a Fetch robot.
study_setting: A laboratory for the live experiment, plus a publicly available recorded dataset (Babble) evaluated offline.
sample_size: 8 participants took part in the live laboratory experiment.
participant_characteristics: The live experiment participants were 8 volunteers from the authors' university campus (7 females, 1 male) who were not paid.
task: In the live experiment, the robot acted as an active listener within an F-formation while participants held informal conversation about topics such as favorite movies and restaurants. A researcher moderator randomly selected a participant to leave the group every 4-5 minutes, and a poster was later brought near the group to test focus shifts to outside objects.
group_size: Live sessions were reported with group sizes ranging from 3 to 7 including the robot. F-formations of size 2 were excluded from testing.
n_robots: One robot (Fetch) per session, which acts as a member of the F-formation.
n_humans: The paper reports group sizes of 3 to 7 including the robot, which implies 2 to 6 humans per session. The paper does not state the human count per session explicitly.
measurement_tools: Accuracy of predicted focus of attention compared with annotated ground truth, using the Babble dataset and manually annotated live-session frames, with a naive voting baseline. Inter-rater agreement between two annotators was also measured with Cohen's kappa.
significant_measures: On the Babble dataset the HMM achieved 81.6% accuracy versus 53.8% for the naive voting baseline. In the live experiment the system reached 94.00% accuracy, and all errors were false negatives.
framing: The paper frames the concept as the group's focus of attention: the visual point at which a majority of participants direct their gaze in a conversation, which the robot detects. It does not use the term robotic gaze-based attention.
framing_definition: The group's focus of attention is defined as the person or object that receives the majority of the attention within or outside the conversational group. It can be a person inside the group, an object inside the group, a person outside the group, or an object outside the group.
framing_role: Knowing the group's focus of attention lets the robot adjust its gaze to the conversational dynamics and behave more naturally. It also gives context that can reduce ambiguity in conversations, such as when two people share a name.
effects: The authors state that the algorithm enabled the robot to exhibit more natural gaze behavior in realistic group interactions. The paper reports no measured effects on human participants or interaction outcomes.
implementation: Autonomous pipeline: Vicon motion capture tracks head position and orientation, REFORM detects F-formations, and an HMM with forward-algorithm updates infers the focus of attention among candidate targets using normally distributed head-orientation likelihoods. A PID controller then turns Fetch's head toward the inferred focus.
embodiment: Fetch, a mobile ground robot with a manipulator. Its head rotates left and right and up and down, and depth and RGB cameras on the head make it look somewhat like it has eyes.
embodiment_influence: The paper does not analyze how the robot's body shaped the study or its effects. Its only embodiment-related remark concerns the built-in attention engines of Nao and Pepper, which the authors judged unsuitable for their research.
tldr: The paper proposes a hidden Markov model that estimates a group's focus of attention from participants' head positions and orientations, so a robot can direct its gaze to the group's focal point, including objects and people outside the group. It reached 81.6% accuracy on the Babble dataset versus a 53.8% baseline, and 94% accuracy in a live Fetch robot experiment with groups of 3 to 7 including the robot.
rqs: RQ1; RQ2; RQ4; RQ5 — The paper defines the group's focus of attention and its categories (RQ1), explains why detecting it matters for multiparty conversational groups (RQ2), describes an HMM and head-control implementation (RQ4), and uses the Fetch robot as its platform (RQ5). It does not study effects of gaze on people (RQ3) or embodiment influence (RQ6).

title: Combining dynamic head pose-gaze mapping with the robot conversational state for attention recognition in human-robot interactions
study_type: Technical/experimental: the authors propose a dynamic Bayesian (IO-HMM) model for visual focus of attention recognition and evaluate it experimentally on the Vernissage dataset.
study_setting: Art exhibition (vernissage) guide scenario with the NAO robot, using a recorded dataset of natural interactions realized with a Wizard of Oz approach.
sample_size: 14 persons (about 140 minutes of data) were retained for the experiments, drawn from the Vernissage dataset of 10 interactions.
task: Nao first engages with the participants and explains three paintings (about 10 minutes per recording on average), then gives the participants a quiz in which they can discuss before answering.
group_size: Two human participants and one robot (NAO) per interaction session.
n_humans: Two human participants per interaction session.
measurement_tools: Frame-based Recognition Rate (percentage of frames with correctly recognized VFOA), with ground truth from annotations and a Vicon motion capture system for head poses and gaze directions.
significant_measures: The dynamic midline model G2 was the best dynamic model, with an average gain of about 13% over the geometric baseline on Vicon head poses (66.6% vs 53.8% full). Using all context cues with G2 reached 72.6% on Vicon data.
framing: Visual focus of attention (VFOA) of people, i.e. what or whom a person is looking at, recognized from head pose.
framing_definition: The authors define VFOA as what or whom a person is looking at, and frame the goal as monitoring people's visual attention relying on head pose.
framing_role: VFOA recognition is described as playing a key role in turn-taking, engagement, intention monitoring, and identifying the addressee in multi-person interaction.
implementation: An Input-Output HMM decodes VFOA from head pose, using dynamic gaze-to-head mapping models and robot dialog context (speaking state, addressee, topic). Head poses come from Vicon or a particle filter tracker on the NAO camera view.
embodiment: Humanoid robot NAO, with a camera in its head used for head pose estimation and an art-guide/quiz-master role.

tldr: The paper proposes a dynamic head-pose-to-gaze mapping and a robot dialog-context prior to improve recognition of people's visual focus of attention in a NAO art-guide scenario with two participants. title: Implementing a gaze control system on a social robot in multi-person interactions
study_type: A technical system description of a gaze control system on the RASA robot, supported by experiments: two calibration experiments with volunteers watching animations and an evaluation with a new group of volunteers comparing robot gaze with participant gaze plus a questionnaire.
study_setting: Laboratory setting. Calibration used computer-animated videos shown on a screen, and the evaluation involved participants interacting freely with the robot and a researcher in the laboratory.
sample_size: 23 volunteers took part in the calibration experiment and 21 different volunteers took part in the evaluation experiment.
participant_characteristics: Students of Sharif University of Technology in Iran. The calibration group had 11 males and 12 females aged 19 to 29, and the evaluation group was aged 19 to 23.
task: In the evaluation, participants watched an 80-second video of two real people entering a room and interacting, then interacted freely with the robot and a researcher while only the gaze control system was active. Calibration used 90-second animations of two characters interacting or telling a story.
group_size: Each evaluation session included one robot (RASA) and two humans: the participant and one researcher.
n_robots: One robot: the RASA humanoid robot.
n_humans: Two humans per evaluation session: the participant and one researcher. The evaluation video showed two real people.
measurement_tools: WebGazer webcam eye tracking was used to record participants' gaze during the animations, and a custom questionnaire built on standard instruments included the Godspeed anthropomorphism questionnaire. Robot gaze was also compared with participants' average gaze pattern.
significant_measures: The robot's gaze matched the average participant gaze pattern for 10 of 13 attention shifts (76.9%) in the 80-second scenario. In the questionnaire, 86% of participants gave a positive score on the statement that the robot sometimes really looked at them, with a mean of 4.33 out of 5.
framing: The paper frames robotic attention as a gaze control system that directs the robot's attention to the most appropriate target in multi-party interactions by selecting an attention target and adjusting the head and eyes.
framing_definition: The authors define gaze as the head and eye movements through which the center of human attention is moved to a specific target.
framing_role: The gaze behaviour selects which person the robot looks at in a multi-person scene, based on social cues and proximity and orientation. It also serves as a deliberate redirection away from the audience and rotates attention so the robot does not fixate on one person.
effects: In the evaluation, the robot's gaze matched participants' average gaze pattern on 10 of 13 attention shifts (76.9%). Also, 86% of the 21 participants gave a positive score that the robot sometimes really looked at them, with a mean of 4.33 out of 5.
implementation: The gaze control system runs as a ROS package within a cognitive architecture. Kinect sensor inputs feed a Perception Unit for social cues, a rule-based Logic Unit selects the target using an elicited attention score, and an Action Unit moves the head and eyes. The gaze shifts are controlled autonomously, with a PID controller for the neck.
embodiment: RASA is a humanoid robot designed for teaching Persian Sign Language. It has 32 degrees of freedom, including 3 neck DOF, and a face projected on an 8-inch screen with adjustable eyes, plus a Kinect sensor in its chest.
embodiment_influence: The authors suggest that the robot's limited embodiment, which performed only eye and head movements, likely explains the average ratings on items about being a living creature, having real feelings, and following social norms.
tldr: The authors implemented a gaze control system on the RASA humanoid robot that chooses which person to look at in multi-person interactions, using social cues and proximity and orientation weights calibrated from human gaze data. In an 80-second real-life scenario the robot's gaze matched participants' average gaze pattern 76.9% of the time, and most participants felt the robot sometimes really looked at them.

title: Embodied Mediation in Group Ideation – A Gestural Robot Can Facilitate Consensus-Building
study_type: Exploratory mixed-methods comparative group study.
study_setting: University laboratory; collaborative vacation-planning sessions conducted in front of a whiteboard.
sample_size: 21 participants: 6 in two reference groups without a robot and 15 in five study groups with a robot.
participant_characteristics: Doctoral and graduate students from a German university’s business and law faculty; 11 male and 10 female, mean age 31 (SD 6.5). Participants did not know their assigned group members, had no prior experience with similar robotic systems, and were familiar with brainstorming.
task: Groups collaboratively planned a feasible five-day vacation trip, generating diverse destinations and activities. Sessions lasted about 30 minutes; individual post-session interviews lasted about 10–15 minutes.
group_size: Four entities per robot session: three human participants and one robot. Reference sessions had three human participants and no robot.
n_robots: One robot in each study group session; none in reference group sessions.
n_humans: Three participants per session.
measurement_tools: Video recordings coded with an extended Interaction Dynamics Notation; individual structured post-session interviews analyzed thematically. No named questionnaire or gaze-tracking instrument is reported.
significant_measures: Groups with the robot spent a greater share of time consensus-building (80% vs. 55%) and less time dissenting (17% vs. 38%) or neutral (3% vs. 7%); group-state distributions differed significantly, χ²(2)=12.9, p<.001. Average session duration did not differ (29.5 vs. 29 minutes).
framing: The paper frames gaze as one of the robot’s nonverbal, gestural mediation behaviors, describing it as directing attention to the active speaker and providing positive attention. It does not give a formal definition of “robotic gaze,” “robotic attention,” or “robotic gaze-based attention.”
framing_definition: The paper does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze or attention. It describes the gaze behavior operationally as following the active speaker and, in the design, turning the robot’s head and moving it toward that speaker.
framing_role: Gaze directed group attention toward the active speaker, offered positive attention and social support, and was intended to encourage participation. Gaze to a less-active member was designed to signal a shift in speaking turns.
effects: Following speakers with gaze was associated with participants moving ideation forward, supporting contributions, and asking clarifying questions. Interviewees described feeling supported and validated, though some felt monitored or judged. Across groups, the robot condition showed more consensus-building and less dissent than the no-robot condition.
implementation: A human operator used Wizard-of-Oz control over a wireless connection, triggering predefined robot gestures based on observed behaviors in a camera feed. The robot’s behaviors included speaker-following gaze and gaze toward the least-active participant.
embodiment: A small, non-humanoid robot built from Lego Mindstorms components with a 3D-printed shell, mounted on a magnetic whiteboard. Its moving head and gaze were used to orient toward people and board entries.
embodiment_influence: The authors state that mounting the robot on the whiteboard gave it a clear vantage point and enabled it to observe and engage with participants; the setup also made its behavior perceptible and able to impact group interaction. The paper does not isolate effects of embodiment from other design features.
tldr: The authors studied groups of three planning a five-day vacation with a small, non-humanoid whiteboard-mounted robot that used gestures including following speakers with gaze. Participants often described the gaze as supportive, and groups with the robot spent more time consensus-building than groups without it; some participants also felt monitored or judged.

title: Assisting Group Discussions Using Desktop Robot Haru
study_type: Experimental user study and technical/system description.
study_setting: University campus recruitment; in-person group discussions at a table with Haru positioned between participants; the gaze policy was trained in Gazebo simulation and evaluated on the physical robot.
sample_size: 40 participants total: 24 in the group-discussion study and 16 teacher-role video evaluators.
participant_characteristics: The discussion participants were 20–25 years old (mean 23.3, SD 1.127); 54.17% male, 33.33% female, and 12.5% undisclosed. They were paired as a “talkative” and a “shy” student. The video evaluators were 21–25 years old (mean 23.5, SD 1.212); 68.75% male, 25% female, and 6.25% undisclosed.
task: Two participants discussed a topic supplied by a staff member acting as a teacher, with Haru assisting. Each group completed three conditions: chatting only; chatting plus dialogue balancing; and chatting, dialogue balancing, and autonomous gaze. Participants familiarized with one another for five minutes beforehand; no discussion duration is specified.
group_size: Three per interaction session: two human participants and one Haru robot.
n_humans: 2 discussion participants per group; the paper considers two users conversing with Haru.
measurement_tools: Godspeed-derived ratings of anthropomorphism, animacy, likability, and perceived intelligence; a custom four-question, 7-point Likert scale; teacher evaluations of discussion videos using the questionnaires; and recorded video. The paper reports no gaze-tracking or behavioral coding instrument.
significant_measures: Student ratings showed significant condition differences across all assessed perspectives (p < 0.01); Condition 3 outperformed Conditions 2 and 1 on Haru’s effectiveness and discussion quality, and Condition 2 outperformed Condition 1 (p < 0.01). Teacher ratings showed the same pattern, except Condition 2 versus 1 differences in animacy and perceived intelligence were near significance (p = 0.03 and p = 0.02).
framing: The authors frame the behavior as “autonomous gazing behavior” and non-verbal gazing behavior, which they associate with politeness and assistance in group discussion. They do not explicitly define “robotic gaze,” “robotic attention,” or “robotic gaze-based attention.”
framing_role: The gaze behavior directs Haru toward the current speaker, toward the middle when both participants are silent or speak simultaneously, and toward the least-spoken participant when Haru encourages her. The authors present this as politeness and as part of assisting group discussion.
effects: With dialogue balancing and autonomous gaze together, participants rated Haru’s effectiveness and discussion quality higher than in the other conditions. The paper attributes increased perceived politeness and discussion quality to the system, but does not isolate gaze’s effect from dialogue balancing in Condition 3.
implementation: The gaze policy used soft actor-critic deep reinforcement learning, trained in Gazebo simulation and transferred to physical Haru. It used user positions and engagement state to select a motor movement angle; Azure Kinect supplied user skeletons and sound locations in the study. The paper describes the behavior as autonomous.
embodiment: Haru is an experimental multimodal desktop robot with five degrees of freedom: base rotation, neck tilt, eye movement, eye rotation, and eye tilt. Its body has addressable LEDs for mouth movements; its eyes contain a 3-inch TFT display bordered by LED strips.
tldr: The authors built a desktop robot system that combines autonomous gaze, dialogue assistance, and verbal prompts to balance participation in two-person discussions. In the study, the combined gaze and dialogue-balancing condition received higher ratings for Haru’s effectiveness and discussion quality, though the study does not isolate gaze’s contribution from the verbal prompts.

title: Towards Robot Autonomy in Group Conversations: Understanding the Effects of Body Orientation and Gaze
study_type: A 2×2 between-subjects experiment, with automated orientation and gaze behaviors and wizard-managed speech and study sequencing.
study_setting: Laboratory room set up for group brainstorming, with 4.4 × 4.4 meters of free space.
sample_size: 69 participants in 20 groups (5 groups per condition).
participant_characteristics: Adults (18 or older), fluent in English, raised in the U.S.; mostly university students. Mean age 24.8 years (SE 1.0); most used computers daily and reported limited robot familiarity. Seven sessions included participants who knew one another.
task: Participants joined a robot-led brainstorming session about useful tasks the robot could perform in the lab. The robot introduced itself, facilitated six minutes of brainstorming, and closed the session; participants wrote ideas on slips and deposited them in color-coded boxes, which prompted natural departures and re-entries. Four conditions crossed middle or attentive orientation with random or attentive gaze.
group_size: Each session involved one robot and three or four human participants (four or five group members total).
n_humans: 3 or 4 participants per session.
measurement_tools: Post-test survey, including the Inclusion of Other in Self (IOS) scale and Williams et al. survey on belongingness and ostracism; Likert ratings of robot impressions. Objective measures included participant–robot distance, group membership, and idea-slip counts. Researchers also used coder annotations of group membership, speaker/addressee transcription, robot eye-fixation inspection, system logs, and teleoperation records.
significant_measures: Attentive gaze (AG) made the robot’s motion seem more natural than random gaze (RG) (M=4.71 vs. 4.00; p<.05). Attentive orientation (AO) increased ratings that the robot looked at participants compared with middle orientation (MO) (M=4.72 vs. 4.11; p<.01). Participants stood farther away with RG than AG during the final brainstorming minute (2.29 m vs. 2.09 m; p=.02); the MO+RG group was farther from the robot than MO+AG (2.40 m vs. 2.03 m; interaction p=.04).
framing: The paper frames gaze as a way for the robot’s eyes to communicate mental states and attention, and examines gaze and body orientation as coupled behaviors in group conversations.
framing_role: Attentive gaze attempts to establish mutual gaze with the person who is the robot’s addressee or current speaker, or with a moving group member when the group is silent. The authors present gaze as communicating attention and contributing to perceived naturalness of robot motion.
effects: Attentive gaze improved perceived naturalness of robot motion and was associated with participants standing closer to the robot than under random gaze. Attentive orientation increased the perception that the robot looked at participants. Gaze and body motion influenced perceptions of one another. The orientation behaviors did not significantly change feelings of inclusion or belonging; the authors report similar feelings for MO and AO.
implementation: The study used an integrated multimodal perception system to track people and the robot, detect conversational groups and the current speaker, and control orientation and gaze. Participants wore baseball caps with UWB beacons; a Kinect contributed skeleton and audio data. The behavior conditions ran autonomously for most of the interaction, while a hidden wizard managed speech and event sequencing and occasionally repositioned or corrected the robot. MO oriented toward the mean direction of group members; AO biased orientation toward the addressee or speaker. AG directed pupils toward the focus of attention, while RG used random small pupil shifts when no scripted eye animation was scheduled.
embodiment: Chester, a mobile furniture platform with a differential-drive base, fixed face, and back-projected eyes.
embodiment_influence: The fixed head meant gaze was manipulated through eye direction, while the robot’s design constrained the behaviors studied. The authors state that its physical appearance and capabilities may have influenced results and behavior design; its differential-drive base limited spatial-behavior complexity and may have affected motion perceptions.
tldr: The authors tested middle versus attentive body orientation and random versus attentive eye gaze with Chester, a mobile robot interacting with groups of three or four people during laboratory brainstorming. Attentive gaze made the robot’s motion seem more natural and led participants to stand closer, while attentive orientation made participants feel that the robot looked at them more; orientation did not significantly alter feelings of group inclusion.

title: Regulating Turn-Taking in Multi-child Spoken Interaction
study_type: Experimental study comparing programmed robot gaze cues with a human moderator.
study_setting: Laboratory setting.
sample_size: 44 children (22 pairs recruited); 19 pairs were included in analysis.
participant_characteristics: Children aged five to nine; 20 female among 44 participants. Children in each pair were familiar siblings or friends and generally similar in age.
task: Pairs played a Disney trivia quiz with directed and open questions, first with a human moderator and then with the robot. Robot questions used either eyes-only or coordinated head-eye cues.
group_size: Three participants per session: two children and one moderator, human or robot.
n_humans: Two children per session; the moderator was either human or robot. Robot sessions also involved a human wizard/experimenter.
measurement_tools: Behavioral video/audio coding by two study-blind annotators; turn-taking, response type, and moderator interruption measures; interface event logs and recordings.
significant_measures: For directed questions, correct turn-taking was 70.0% with robot head-eye cues versus 51.4% with eyes-only; eyes-only produced significantly more errors than head-eyes (χ²=9.272, p=.002) and human natural movement (χ²=8.73, p=.003). In open questions, head-eyes produced the most even participation distribution; the paper does not report a significance test for that comparison.
framing: Gaze is framed as the combination of eye and head movement and as a nonvocal cue for regulating turn-taking and identifying addressees.
framing_definition: The paper explicitly defines gaze as the combination of eye and head movement; it does not give a separate definition of robotic attention.
framing_role: Gaze cues regulate turn-taking and signal the intended addressee or inclusion of both children.
effects: Coordinated head-eye movement improved children’s directed turn-taking accuracy over eyes-only cues, reaching performance comparable to the human moderator. In open questions, head-eyes yielded the most balanced participation; eye-only cues were associated with more imbalance and fewer ties.
implementation: A dialog system used a Kinect person-tracking module to locate the two players and direct robot gaze. A human wizard supplied high-level input; programmed cues were eyes-only or coordinated eye and head movement.
embodiment: Sammy, an anthropomorphic robot head with an adult-like form, rear-projected facial animation on a 3D-printed mask, and a two-degree-of-freedom neck.
embodiment_influence: The authors report that eye movement alone on this anthropomorphic head did not reliably signal addressee to young children, while prominent head rotation in coordinated gaze supported turn regulation. They compare this with adult studies using the same robot head.
tldr: The study tested gaze cues during trivia games with pairs of children and a human or robot moderator. Robot head-eye cues supported directed turn-taking as well as the human moderator, while eye movement alone led to more errors; head-eye cues also produced the most balanced participation on open questions.
rqs: RQ1; RQ2; RQ3; RQ4; RQ5; RQ6 — The paper frames gaze as coordinated eye and head movement, studies its role in turn-taking and addressee signaling, and measures effects on children’s responses and participation. title: When a Robot Is Your Teammate
study_type: Conceptual framework paper presenting four use cases from previous work, including experimental user studies and a technical system description.
study_setting: The paper describes multiple settings: an online video-rating study and game-based human–robot interaction studies; the setting for all studies is not specified.
task: Tasks included playing a four-player trick-taking card game in two human–robot teams, a collective-risk musical-band game, and watching scripted videos of a silent coordination task to rate teamwork. Durations are not stated.
group_size: Groups varied by use case: four members (two humans and two robots) or three members (one human and two robots). The gaze study used a triadic team of one robot and two humans.
n_robots: Two robots per group in the card-game and musical-band studies; one robot in the gaze study.
n_humans: Two humans in the card-game study; one human in the musical-band study; two humans in the gaze study.
measurement_tools: For the gaze study, participants rated coordination, fluency, teammate traits, and work alliance using Hoffman’s measure. The paper also describes other use-case measures, including the Godspeed questionnaire, trust and group-identification scales, preference choices, and behavioral coding based on Bales Interaction Process Analysis.
significant_measures: In the gaze study, both responsive and attentive gaze improved perceived teammate perception and team fluency versus baseline; attentive gaze was rated more fluent than responsive gaze. Teams where both humans displayed gaze were rated more coordinated, fluent, and united than teams where only one human did so. Statistical values are not provided.
framing: Robotic teammate gaze behavior is framed as a nonverbal behavior supporting task cohesion through joint attention and structural cohesion through signaling roles and communication structures.
framing_definition: The paper does not give a standalone definition of robotic gaze or robotic gaze-based attention; it describes responsive and attentive gaze strategies by what gaze targets they detect and how the robot responds.
framing_role: Gaze supports mutual gaze and joint attention, conveys communication structure and roles, and is examined as a means to affect team coordination and fluency.
effects: Responsive and attentive gaze positively affected perceived teammate quality and team fluency; attentive gaze yielded higher perceived fluency than responsive gaze. More human teammates displaying gaze was associated with higher perceived coordination, fluency, and unity.
implementation: An autonomous gaze system detects human teammates’ gaze. In the responding-gaze condition, the robot detects gaze toward itself and looks back at that person. In the attentive-gaze condition, it also detects gaze between human teammates and looks at the same person they are looking at. The baseline only blinks.
embodiment_influence: The paper states that gaze response depends on the communication structure the robot perceives, and more generally that embodiment affords different ways of expressing emotion. It does not describe a specific robot platform or explain how the gaze-study robot’s body affected the study or results.
tldr: This paper presents cohesion as a framework for designing, developing, and evaluating robotic teammates and reviews four prior use cases. In its multiparty gaze study, autonomous responsive and attentive gaze improved perceived teamwork, with attentive gaze rated as more fluent than responsive gaze.

title: Meet me where i'm gazing: how shared attention gaze affects human-robot handover timing
study_type: Human-human observational handover study followed by a controlled human-robot paired-comparison experiment.
study_setting: Controlled room during a university orientation event.
sample_size: The human-robot experiment recruited 102 volunteers; data from 96 participants were analyzed. The human-human study included 12 volunteers.
participant_characteristics: The human-robot experiment analyzed 96 participants (63 male, 33 female; mean age 23, SD 5.59); participants were recruited as naïve volunteers. The human-human study had 12 volunteers (10 male, 2 female).
task: Participants received a water bottle handed over by the PR2 under two gaze conditions per participant, then placed the bottle in a box and returned for a second handover. The experiment compared no gaze, shared-attention gaze toward the handover location, and turn-taking gaze that shifted from the handover location to the participant’s face.
group_size: Two per human-robot interaction: one robot and one participant.
n_humans: 1 participant per human-robot handover interaction.
measurement_tools: Measures included video-based frame-by-frame coding of human-human giver gaze; infrared motion sensors for participant reach time; robot event timestamps; and a custom post-handover questionnaire comparing preference, naturalness, and perceived timing communication.
significant_measures: Participants reached for the object earlier with shared-attention gaze than with no gaze (M=1.91 vs. 2.54 seconds; p<.005). No significant reach-time differences were found between shared-attention and turn-taking gaze or between turn-taking and no gaze. Subjective comparisons showed trends favoring turn-taking gaze, but no significant overall differences.
framing: The paper frames its behavior as robot gaze during handovers, including shared-attention gaze at the projected handover location and turn-taking gaze that adds a look toward the receiver’s face.
framing_definition: The paper defines deictic gaze or shared visual attention as one person following another’s direction of attention to look at a fixed point in space.
framing_role: Shared-attention gaze is intended to direct the human’s attention to the projected handover location and convey where the handover will take place. The added look to the receiver’s face was tested as a timing cue and as a way to improve subjective experience.
effects: Shared-attention gaze led participants to reach for the offered object significantly earlier than no gaze, with mean reach occurring before the robot finished moving. Turn-taking gaze showed trends toward better preference, naturalness, and timing judgments in some comparisons.
implementation: The PR2 expressed gaze through head orientation. The robot tracked its end-effector while acquiring the bottle, then changed gaze during the transition from ready position to handover location; software modules controlled the arm and head, and a sensor array detected participant reach.
embodiment: The study used a PR2 humanoid mobile robotic platform with a pan-tilt head and two 7-DOF arms, each with a two-fingered, 1-DOF gripper.
tldr: The authors tested three PR2 gaze conditions during one-to-one bottle handovers: no gaze, gaze toward the handover location, and gaze that then shifted to the participant’s face. Participants reached significantly earlier with shared-attention gaze than with no gaze; turn-taking gaze showed some nonsignificant favorable trends in subjective ratings.

title: Deliberate delays during robot-to-human handovers improve compliance with gaze communication
study_type: Experimental study
study_setting: In-person human–robot interaction experiment in Pittsburgh; the paper does not explicitly label the setting as a laboratory.
sample_size: 32 participants
participant_characteristics: 18 female participants; mean age 34; recruited from the Pittsburgh area through Carnegie Mellon University's online participant pool.
task: Participants took part in a block-sorting handover task. HERB handed them five colored blocks; participants sorted each into a yellow or blue box according to their preference. For ambiguous and semi-ambiguous blocks, HERB suggested a box by looking toward it. The interaction lasted about 2 minutes 20 seconds.
group_size: One robot and one participant per interaction session.
n_humans: 1 participant per interaction session
measurement_tools: Task performance (whether participants followed HERB’s suggestions); custom written post-task questionnaires, including free-response and Likert-scale items; semi-structured interviews; and video recordings coded for looking at HERB’s face/head and noticing suggestions. No named standardized questionnaire or eye tracker is reported.
significant_measures: Handover delay increased compliance with HERB’s semi-ambiguous-block suggestion (19% without delay versus 63% with delay; χ²(1, N=32)=6.77, p=0.0092), increased head-looking time (24.7 versus 50.6 seconds; F(1,31)=12.9828, p=0.0012), and increased self-reported recognition of suggestions (75% versus 38%; p=0.0302). Gaze type did not significantly affect compliance.
framing: The paper frames robotic eye gaze as a non-verbal communication channel that can provide information and influence human motor behavior. Its focal use is a gaze cue that suggests where a handed-over object should be sorted.
framing_definition: The authors do not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze or robotic attention. They describe gaze communication as non-verbal communication and operationalize the cue as the robot orienting its head toward a box.
framing_role: The robot’s gaze communicates a sorting suggestion about where to put the object after the handover. A deliberate release delay is used to redirect human attention toward the robot’s head so people notice the gaze cue.
effects: The delay increased attention to HERB’s head, recognition of gaze suggestions, and compliance with counterintuitive suggestions. The social-gaze manipulation (joint attention versus mirrored gaze) did not significantly affect attention or compliance.
implementation: HERB used pre-scripted trajectories and a force/torque sensor to detect when the participant grasped the block. On each trial it turned its head toward a box; in the delay condition it released only after completing the head turn, while in the no-delay condition release and head turn began simultaneously. The experiment ran autonomously with real-time force feedback; no real-time vision was used.
embodiment: HERB (Home Exploring Robot Butler) is a bimanual assistive robot with two 7-DOF WAM arms, each with a 4-DOF three-finger Barrett hand. It has a pan-tilt head with a Microsoft Kinect and camera; the visible round cameras on the Kinect front serve as its eyes. Only the right arm was used.
embodiment_influence: The authors suggest that HERB’s relatively abstract, non-anthropomorphic head may have affected how well participants perceived joint attention; they propose that a robot with more defined eyes might yield different results. The paper reports no significant effect of gaze type in this study.
tldr: In a one-person block-sorting task with HERB, the robot suggested a box by looking toward it during an object handover. Delaying release increased participants’ attention to HERB’s head, recognition of the gaze suggestions, and compliance; the joint-attention versus mirrored-gaze manipulation had no significant effect.

Its single-human sessions do not directly study multiparty interaction, so its relevance to the review’s multiparty questions is indirect.

title: Multi-party Interaction with a Robot Receptionist
study_type: Within-subjects video-based experiment comparing four robot engagement policies, followed by an online questionnaire.
study_setting: Online questionnaire study using video demonstrations; the interaction depicted is a robot receptionist scenario.
sample_size: 110 submissions were considered in the analysis, from 120 recruited participants.
participant_characteristics: Participants were aged 18–65 and recruited through Prolific. The paper states they had no health issues that might affect their feedback, including bad vision, bad hearing, cognitive impairment, or mental illness.
task: Participants watched four randomized video recordings of a robot receptionist interacting with two users under four engagement policies, then completed a questionnaire after each video.
group_size: Three entities in the depicted interaction: one robot and two users.
n_humans: 2 users in the depicted interaction.
measurement_tools: Custom online questionnaire with five-point Likert ratings, based on Godspeed questionnaire items for anthropomorphism, animacy, and perceived intelligence; analyzed using Friedman tests and pairwise Mann–Whitney U tests.
significant_measures: Ratings differed across all four policies for all eight measured variables (Friedman p < .001). Policy 4, combining eye gaze, head pose, and speech, was rated more positively than Policy 1 for intelligence and respect for social norms (both pairwise p = 0.01); the paper also reports consciousness higher for Policy 3 than Policy 1 (p = 0.03), though the results paragraph inconsistently describes the comparison as Policy 2. Policy 3 received the lowest politeness rating, while Policy 4 was rated as polite as Policy 1.
framing: The paper frames eye gaze and head pose as cues used with speech to manage attention and coordinate turn-taking in multiparty interaction; it does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze or robotic attention.
framing_role: Gaze and head pose acknowledge a newly arriving user and, together with speech, help coordinate turn-taking and manage multiparty engagement.
effects: Eye gaze was associated with higher perceived intelligence than the neutral policy; head pose was associated with higher perceived consciousness than the neutral policy. The combined gaze, head pose, and speech policy was associated with greater perceived adherence to social norms. Head pose without speech was rated lowest for politeness, while the combined policy was perceived as polite as the neutral policy.
implementation: The system uses robot vision and speech-recognition input for scene analysis, reasons about the physical surroundings and engagement choices, then executes coordinated gestures, facial expressions, and head movements synchronized with speech. Policies vary whether eye gaze, head pose, and speech are used when a second user enters; Furhat is the robot platform.
embodiment: Furhat robot; the paper describes it as a robot receptionist but does not state further physical features.
embodiment_influence: The authors contrast their three-dimensional robot with an earlier on-screen avatar, noting that the avatar inhibits certain social cues such as mutual gaze and can create confusion about where the system is looking. They do not report an embodiment comparison in this study.
tldr: The paper compares four video-based robot receptionist policies for coordinating turn-taking with two users, varying eye gaze, head pose, and speech.
