title: Model for controlling a target human's attention in multi-party settings
study_type: Experimental study with two experiments and a technical system description.
study_setting: University experimental setting; the paper describes participant pairs seated and interacting with robot heads in an arranged room setup. It does not explicitly label the setting as a laboratory.
sample_size: Experiment 1: 20 participants in 10 pairs. Experiment 2: 36 graduate students.
participant_characteristics: Experiment 1 participants were 15 males and 5 females, average age 27.92 years, recruited from Saitama University. Experiment 2 participants were graduate students, mean age 26.5 years (SD 3.4).
task: Experiment 1: pairs played a card game while perceiving a robot head’s turning or shaking motions. Experiment 2: pairs looked around at paintings while the robot attempted to attract a selected target’s attention and direct it toward a left or right table object; there were two trials per pair.
group_size: Each interaction session involved two humans and two robot heads: one moving or attention-control robot and one stationary robot.
n_humans: 2 participants per session.
measurement_tools: Custom 1–7 rating questionnaires; paired t-tests for the first experiment; video observation for time to attention shift and success ratio; ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey tests for experiment 2 questionnaire and timing results.
significant_measures: In experiment 1, head shaking attracted more attention than head turning in the far peripheral field of view (FPFOV; p < .0001 for both participants); head turning was sufficient in the near peripheral field of view, and neither motion attracted attention out of view. In experiment 2, the proposed method had shorter time to attention shift (1.72 s) and higher success ratio (58.3%) than methods 2 (2.71 s; 25%) and 3 (1.80 s; 33%); timing differences were significant between methods 1 and 2 (p = .0076) and methods 2 and 3 (p < .05), but not methods 1 and 3. Proposed method ratings supported eye contact, intended attention direction, and conveying non-communicative intention to non-targets.
framing: The paper frames its approach as a five-phase attention control process for directing a particular human’s attention among multiple people, using non-verbal robot behaviors.
framing_definition: The authors define attention control as gaze (head) control that shifts someone’s gaze from one direction to another intended by the initiator.
framing_role: The process selects and engages a target person, establishes eye contact, signals non-communicative intent to non-targets, and directs the target’s attention to a referential object.
effects: Robot head motions attracted attention depending on the target’s viewing position: turning worked in near peripheral view, shaking was needed in far peripheral view, and non-verbal motions could not attract someone out of view. In the second experiment, eye blinking and gaze back were associated with faster, more successful attention shifts and stronger perceived eye contact; looking away helped non-targets perceive less communicative intent.
implementation: The system uses a finite-state-machine model, head and body tracking, situation and face detection, eye blinking, and pan-tilt control. It turns toward the target, shakes its head if needed, waits about four seconds for a response, blinks after face detection, avoids a non-target by turning away, returns its gaze if the target responds, and shifts gaze/head toward the object.
embodiment: A custom robot head with spherical 3D mask, projected CG eyes, laser range sensor, three USB cameras, and pan-tilt unit.
embodiment_influence: The authors state that the robot heads’ human-face-like appearance could itself attract participants, even without robot actions; the study used a static robot as a comparison for this reason.
tldr: The paper proposes and tests a five-phase, non-verbal model for directing one person’s attention in a multiparty interaction. Experiments with paired participants and robot heads indicate that head motion effectiveness depends on viewing position, while blinking, gaze avoidance, and gaze back can help the robot engage a target, shift their attention, and signal disinterest in non-targets.

title: Entrainment Effect Caused by Joint Attention of Two Robots
study_type: Experimental study with two experiments.
study_setting: In-person laboratory-style experiment; the paper describes a controlled setup but does not explicitly name the setting.

participant_characteristics: 17 male and 3 female participants; no age or prior robot experience is stated.
task: Experiment 1: participants watched two robots converse and then jointly gaze at an object, then guessed the object's color and conversation content. Experiment 2: participants watched synchronous or asynchronous joint gaze and identified the target object's color over 13 trials. Duration is not stated.
group_size: Three individuals per interaction: two robots and one human participant.
measurement_tools: SMI eye-tracking glasses; custom questionnaires; participant responses identifying target colors and conversation content; target identification accuracy and distance from the correct object.
significant_measures: Participants in Condition 1-A (robots gazed at the participant before shifting to an object) followed the robots' gaze more than in Condition 1-B (p .05) and tended to be more immersed in communication. framing_role: Joint gaze is framed as supporting shared recognition of a target and entraining or immersing a person in group communication.
effects: When both robots gazed at a person before gazing at an object, participants followed their gaze more and tended to be more immersed in communication. title: Cooperative gazing behaviors in human multi-robot interaction
study_type: Experimental behavioral study with a real-time gaze-contingent platform; includes a technical system description.
study_setting: University laboratory setting; participants interacted with robots at a table. The paper does not explicitly label the study as a laboratory study.
sample_size: 21 participants included in the two conditions: 10 in the active-following condition and 11 in the passive-following condition. Five additional participants were excluded due to technical issues.
participant_characteristics: Undergraduate students at Indiana University; age and gender are not reported in the provided paper text.
task: Participants taught two robots the names of four novel, single-colored objects per trial, using artificial two-syllable names. They completed three trials of about three minutes each. The active-following condition paired a stereotype robot with an active robot; the passive-following condition paired a stereotype robot with a passive robot.
group_size: Three agents per session: one human participant and two robots.
n_humans: 1 human participant per session; the paper describes each participant interacting with the two robots.
measurement_tools: Head-mounted Eye-Trac 6000 eye tracker and real-time gaze/ROI tracking; recorded first-person videos, robot head movements and gaze directions, and participant speech. Utterances were segmented by a speech-silence endpoint detection algorithm and transcribed by three human coders. Robot gaze behavior and successful gaze-following rates were also evaluated. Post-experiment interviews are mentioned, with no instrument specified.
significant_measures: Participants looked more frequently at the active robot than at the passive robot (p = 0.03); they produced more spoken utterances in the active-following condition (26.45 vs. 20.71; p = 0.03). Around naming events, participants in the passive-following condition made more shifts between different objects than those in the active-following condition (before: F(1,59) = 127.69, p < 0.0001; after: F(1,59) = 350.52, p < 0.0001).
framing: The authors frame the topic as cooperative gazing behavior in human multi-robot interaction, including robot gaze behaviors contingent on the human’s attention. They identify following the user’s gaze, actively directing the user’s gaze, and encouraging attention toward other robots as possible cooperative behaviors.
framing_definition: Cooperative behavior is defined as an action performed by robots that are not capturing the user’s direct attention. The paper does not provide a distinct formal definition of robotic gaze, robotic attention, or robotic gaze-based attention.
framing_role: Robot gaze behaviors can elicit or redirect the user’s attention, coordinate attention between the human and robots, and shape group communication and teaching behaviors. The active robot’s face looks were intended to attract the teacher’s attention when the teacher looked at its peer.
effects: Participants were sensitive to distinct robot cooperative gaze behaviors: active gaze elicited more frequent face looks and more speech utterances, while passive gaze did not direct more attention to its robot peer and was associated with less attention to the passive robot. Active-following participants also showed fewer object-to-object attention shifts around naming events, which the authors characterize as better teaching signals. No significant difference was found in object-look duration or naming-event counts between conditions.
implementation: A gaze-contingent system used a head-mounted eye tracker and first-person video to detect the participant’s gaze target among four objects and two robots. A robot control unit received the target ROI; each robot’s control was independent. Robots followed gaze after a buffer of 30 gaze data points, requiring more than 50% to indicate the same ROI. Reported mean response time was 657 ms. Robot behaviors were programmed as stereotype, active, or passive strategies; no Wizard-of-Oz control is described.
embodiment: Two Nao humanoid robots manufactured by Aldebaran Robotics; the Nao has 25 degrees of freedom and a CMOS eye camera.
tldr: The authors tested two Nao robots interacting with one human who taught them object names, while the robots used different gaze strategies triggered by the human’s attention. Participants responded to those strategies: the active robot received more face looks, and active-following sessions produced more speech utterances and fewer attention shifts between objects around naming events.

title: Are you looking at me? Perception of robot attention is mediated by gaze type and group size
study_type: Experimental mixed between- and within-subjects study, with a technical platform description.
study_setting: Laboratory experiment.
sample_size: 53 participants took part; 51 were analyzed after two were excluded.
participant_characteristics: 20 male and 33 female participants; age, population, and prior robot experience are not stated.
task: Participants watched groups of robots perform random movements and occasional gaze fixations, then identified which robot appeared to be paying attention to them and rated their confidence. They completed 30 trials, each lasting 30 seconds, across fixation durations of 0, 1, 3, or 6 seconds.
group_size: Each session included one participant and either 4, 6, or 8 robots.
n_humans: One participant per session.
measurement_tools: Custom trial-level robot-choice responses and a 0–100 confidence rating; accuracy of identifying the target robot was analyzed.
significant_measures: Identification accuracy was significantly higher for 1- and 3-second fixations than for 0- or 6-second fixations. Accuracy differed by group size; the four-robot group outperformed the eight-robot group, with four versus six robots marginal. Overall accuracy across fixation durations was 37%, 28%, and 26% for groups of four, six, and eight robots, respectively.
framing: The authors frame the study as perception and detection of robot visual attention, operationalized through robot gaze fixations directed at the participant. They call their approach a “sociophysical level of analysis.”
framing_definition: The paper operationalizes an attention fixation as a gaze fixation directed at the user; it does not provide a broader formal definition of robotic gaze or attention.
framing_role: Robot gaze fixations are used to convey or indicate that the robot is attending to the participant; the experiment tests whether participants can detect that attention among distractor robots.
effects: Multiple short fixations were more accurately recognized as attention than fewer, longer fixations. Increasing the number of distractor robots reduced accuracy.
implementation: The researchers modified MyKeepon toys for computer control using Arduino Uno boards and motor shields. Robot motions were pre-scripted and sent over USB/serial; motor commands were cached on the boards and played sequentially. Target robots were hand-calibrated to orient toward participants.
embodiment: Programmable MyKeepon toys: small, yellow, snowman-like robots with two eyes and a nose and four degrees of freedom, controlled by three DC motors.
embodiment_influence: The robots’ imprecise motors made perfectly direct gaze difficult, so target gaze was oriented toward or near participants; the authors note that gaze offset may have contributed to generally low accuracy. The body moves as a whole to orient gaze.
tldr: The authors built programmable MyKeepon robots and tested whether people could identify which robot was looking toward them in groups of four, six, or eight. Participants identified attention more accurately when fixations were short and frequent, and accuracy declined as robot group size increased.
rqs: RQ1; RQ2; RQ3; RQ4; RQ5; RQ6 — The paper operationalizes attention through gaze fixations directed at the participant, tests attention detection in multi-robot groups, and reports effects of fixation timing and group size. It also describes the robot control implementation and platform, including how motor imprecision and whole-body gaze affected the study.

title: A considerate care robot able to serve in multi-party settings
study_type: Technical/system description with a controlled comparative experiment and ethnographic observations.
study_setting: An experimental room with participants seated in chairs; the robot’s mobility was also tested moving around tables and obstacles. The paper additionally reports observations at a Japanese elderly day-care center.
sample_size: 40 participants.
participant_characteristics: Undergraduate students in the university’s Faculty of Liberal Arts; the paper does not state their age, gender, or prior robot experience.
task: Participants played person B, called the robot by raising a hand after it began moving to person A, and experienced either gaze acknowledgment or no gaze acknowledgment. The robot delivered snacks to two people, serving A before B.
group_size: Two humans and one robot per experimental interaction.
measurement_tools: Four custom 1–7 response questions; a 28-pair Semantic Differential impression evaluation on seven-degree scales; video analysis/counting of hand raises and observed calling behaviors; statistical comparison of question scores. WoZ was used to avoid request recognition errors.
significant_measures: Gaze acknowledgment produced higher average scores on all four questions, with significant differences for perceived recognition (Q2) and ease of calling (Q3), p<0.05; Q4 satisfaction did not differ significantly. Participants without gaze acknowledgment raised their hands more than once, while the participant shown after gaze acknowledgment put her hand down.
framing: The paper frames gaze as a nonverbal acknowledgment that projects the order of service provision and signals which requester will be served next.
framing_role: Gaze acknowledges a subsequent request, projects the service order, and communicates to the waiting person that they will be served next, allowing the robot to continue serving the first person while the second waits.
effects: Gaze acknowledgment improved perceived robot recognition and ease of calling; participants gave higher scores across all four questions, though satisfaction did not differ significantly. Without acknowledgment, participants repeated hand raises and some used emphatic waving or said “excuse me.” Impression ratings also suggested more positive evaluation with the nonverbal gesture.
implementation: CCR autonomously circulates while looking around, detects hand-raising requests using a body-mounted laser range finder and human-shape tracking, and, when a second request is detected en route to the first person, momentarily stops and turns its gaze toward the second person before continuing. The comparative experiment used WoZ to avoid request-recognition errors.
embodiment: CCR used a Segway RMP50 mobile platform, an upper body with eight arm-motion joints, and a pan-tilt mount in the neck for head movement.
tldr: The authors developed a mobile care robot that acknowledges a second person’s request by turning its gaze toward them while it is serving someone else. In a two-person snack-delivery experiment, gaze acknowledgment improved perceived recognition and ease of calling, while satisfaction ratings did not differ significantly.
